---
title: "Necessary Response"
author: "DK"
date: "2026-07-19"
categories: [communication]
---

One of the most valuable lessons I’ve learned over the years is that when someone begins a discussion with you, they are not always looking for advice, possible solutions, or even answers.

More often than not, they simply want to be heard and understood.

Over time, you realize they have already formulated their own answers—they just needed a sounding board.

The real challenge, however, isn't learning how to listen; it's learning how to decipher.

It’s knowing when a conversation requires a thoughtful reply (**RSVP**) versus when it’s an **NRN**—*No Response Necessary*.

It sounds simple, but navigating that distinction in real time—knowing when to offer perspective and when to simply nod and hold space—is a delicate balance.

I am still figuring that part out.

![](images/20260702_124137.jpg)

---

For a long time, I operated under an implicit assumption: whether because of my position, my role, or simply my age, I felt an obligation to be the solution provider. When someone brought a problem to me, my instinct was to solve it.

Recently, though, I have been re-evaluating the true impact and value of listening, offering advice, and providing quiet reinforcement.

The person in front of me has almost certainly thought through their situation more thoroughly than I have in a brief conversation.

My role shouldn't be to jump in with a quick response or a ready-made answer.

Instead, I’ve started thinking of my role like a contestant on *Jeopardy!*.

Rather than blurting out a quick answer to beat an imaginary timer, the goal is to frame things through the right questions—understanding the category, uncovering what truly matters, and steadily climbing toward the heavier, deeper questions that help check off what needs to be explored.

Because, in life as on *Jeopardy!*, the best solution provider is seldom the person who rushes out the answers.

It’s the person who helps you ask the right questions.

![](images/20260708_201907.jpg)

---

Artificial Intelligence can now provide instant, ready-made answers on almost any topic conceivable. Many of its answers are far more complete and structured than the ones I gave earlier in my life.

The more an AI gets to know the questioner, the more tailored and relevant its responses become.

And yet, I am not ready to surrender my role as the one who asks the questions rather than the one who tries to provide all the answers.

AI and Large Language Models will continue to advance and expand at an unimaginable pace, but there is one domain where human beings still hold a distinct edge: the nature of our questions.

We have the capacity to ask questions that are not meant to extract data or elicit quick solutions, but rather to reveal our shared humanity—questions that show we are vulnerable, and that acknowledge our own answers are inherently limited.

In this life, we will always have more questions than we have answers.

And if a moment ever comes when we feel we have more answers than questions, perhaps that is our signal to reset—and to start asking what it truly means to be a human.

대답하라 or *Répondez s'il vous plaît.*
